meta.regime: Both of the shocks this board has been trading reversed inside twenty-four hours, and they reversed against each other again. The AI capital-spending repricing stopped being a commodity story and became an equity one: the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36%, or 1,807 points, to 26,629.81 on Thursday, erasing roughly 2.3 trillion dollars on fears that the Democratic sweep stalls the data-centre buildout, the Dow lost more than 1,800 points and the Russell 2000 fell 4.45%. That pulled the ten-year to about 4.837%, a two-month low against an October high of 5.36%, and knocked December Fed hike odds from roughly 82% to 66-68%. At the same time the energy de-escalation trade unwound: Brent is back at 99.862 and plus 1.60%, WTI 91.648 and plus 1.25%, EU gas 92.48 and plus 1.99%, UK gas 230.35 and plus 2.41%, all on fresh Hormuz tanker attacks. So the haven bid is back on both legs at once, and the franc has now beaten all seven other currencies on the day and on the week while the Australian dollar has lost to all seven two days running.
meta.nextBigEvent: United States and Canadian employment in the same minute today, Friday November 6 at 13:30Z - the last payrolls before the December 9 FOMC. US non-farm payrolls are forecast at plus 65,000 after plus 29,000, unemployment held at 4.2% and average hourly earnings plus 0.3% after plus 0.1%; Canadian employment is forecast at plus 14,600 after minus 68,300 with unemployment held at 6.5%. Ueda speaks at 16:00Z and New Zealand votes Saturday.

dailyRead: Yesterday this file argued that six of these eight central banks had built hawkish cases on an energy input that had just fallen 12% to 15% in five sessions, and that the risk to forward paths was therefore dovish everywhere except the United States. Half of that call has to be withdrawn today, and the honest thing is to say which half and why. The energy leg reversed. Brent is 99.862 and plus 1.60% on the day, back from 94.106 twenty-four hours ago - a 6.1% round trip - and WTI is 91.648 and plus 1.25%, up from 87.186, so the single-session break that looked like the end of the Hormuz regime has retraced more than a third of itself in two sessions. The gas complex went with it and went harder: EU gas is 92.48 and plus 1.99% against 85.18 yesterday, German gas 92.13 and plus 2.84%, UK gas 230.35 and plus 2.41%, and while all three are still down 7% to 11% on the week they are now up 18% to 20% on the month. The reason is not a change of mind about diplomacy, it is ordnance: the IRGC says two tankers and a tugboat were burned in the Strait, and on the same day Iran said it could reopen Hormuz within two days if its demands on sanctions and frozen assets were met, with Qatar mediating and Iran's foreign minister meeting Saudi and Qatari officials. The market is being asked to price a reopening and an escalation simultaneously, which is why crude is a range at 91 and not a directional trade in either direction. What this does to the board is reverse yesterday's dovish lean on the energy-dependent currencies rather than confirm it. Bailey made the next Bank of England increase conditional in one sentence - unless there is progress towards resolving the conflict, a further increase in Bank Rate may be warranted - and UK gas is up 2.41% today and 18.97% on the month, so the condition he named is arming again rather than disarming. The euro area's 4.0% October HICP was delivered by energy at 20.8%, and Lagarde said in Milan on Thursday that the Governing Council is watching the indirect effects of the energy shock tied to the Iran war; euro-area gas up 18.44% on the month is that shock continuing. Macklem's Middle East energy shock is 4.5% off its low. The franc's 1.5% October CPI, which this file downgraded yesterday precisely because it was roughly 96% energy, is a better forward case today than it was then. Second, and this is the half of yesterday's call that did not just survive but inverted, the United States. The dollar's hawkish case was described here yesterday as the only one on the board that never rested on energy, and that remains true - CPI 3.7%, core 2.6%, two October dissents for a hike - but the case got shorter anyway, from the other side. The AI capital-spending repricing had been a commodity and sentiment story; on Thursday it became an equity event. The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36%, 1,807 points, to 26,629.81, erasing roughly 2.3 trillion dollars of value; the Dow lost more than 1,800 points, about 3.4%; the Russell 2000 fell 4.45%; Micron fell around 12% intraday and Qualcomm's weak smartphone-chip sales added to it. The index is in correction and it was the worst session since the April 2025 tariff panic. The trigger was the midterm result being re-read: Democrats took both chambers and also the Texas and Ohio governorships, which are among the most intense data-centre development areas in the country, so the trade went from relief on deficit expansion to fear of regulatory drag on AI infrastructure in a single session. The rates consequence is the thing to trade. The ten-year fell to about 4.837%, a two-month low, and December Fed hike odds fell to 66-68% on CME FedWatch from 82% a day earlier, with Kalshi and Polymarket near 66% and a hold near 31%. This file carried 76% to 82% yesterday. That is a reversal inside a day, it is not noise, and the specific fact that changed is the equity rout and the yield move it caused - not a data point, and not anything the Fed said. Which leaves the dollar in an exact mirror of yesterday's position: twenty-four hours ago the price was weak and the rate case was firming, today the price is firm, with DXY at 101.757 and plus 0.15% and the dollar beating five of seven, while the rate case is fading. The score stays at zero because the two legs still offset; what changed is which leg is which, and payrolls at 13:30Z is where it breaks. Third, the currencies the risk-off actually paid. The franc is the cleanest read on this board: it gained against all seven others on the day and against all seven on the week, EUR/CHF is 0.91388 and minus 0.78% on the week, AUD/CHF minus 3.19%, NZD/CHF minus 2.30%, CAD/CHF minus 1.59%, and it sits near its highest since mid-September. It has both legs for the first time in a fortnight - equities in correction and the Strait being attacked again - and the inflation leg that was cut yesterday is partly repaired by the energy rebound. It goes to plus two. The ceiling is the Swiss National Bank rather than the data: Schlegel said on Thursday that the policy rate remains the main tool and that the bank has not yet seen significant second-round inflation effects, no near-term hike is expected at zero, and Commerzbank notes EUR/CHF is approaching levels where the SNB has previously threatened stronger intervention. That is why the franc crosses are sized as high conviction only where the other leg is independently broken. The yen is bid but it is the more conflicted haven. It gained against the euro, sterling, the Aussie, the Kiwi and the Canadian dollar and lost marginally to the dollar and the franc, with USD/JPY at 157.776, and December is roughly 80% priced in swaps with more than 80% of economists looking for 1.50% on December 18. The tension is specific: Ueda's reasoning for tightening leaned on strong global AI demand, and global AI demand is exactly what lost 2.3 trillion dollars of equity value on Thursday and what ANZ now blames for copper. The yen is being bought as a haven against the breaking of its own hike premise, which is why it stays at plus one and MIXED rather than being upgraded, and why Ueda at 16:00Z matters more than usual. Fourth, the currencies it punished, where the cleanest trades are. The Australian dollar lost to all seven other currencies for a second consecutive day, is minus 2.15% on the week, and printed a three-week low below 0.70 at 0.68810. The mechanism is explicit rather than inferred: copper is 6.1867, minus 1.00% on the day, minus 4.21% on the week and minus 6.21% on the month, and ANZ attributes the weakness to the technology selloff weighing on sentiment - which is the AI-related demand for technology goods that the RBA itself cited in its November 3 statement being priced out in public. Against that the RBA holds the highest cash rate on the board at 4.85%, hiked on a 6-3 vote with three members preferring a hold, and softened its commitment to further tightening. A top rate that the market will not pay for, with the demand leg under it being dismantled, is a short, and it goes to minus two. The Kiwi sits alongside it at minus two with a different problem: Citi has now scrapped its RBNZ hike forecasts entirely and expects rates on hold through 2027, against Commerzbank still looking for December and the first quarter and ANZ looking for three consecutive increases, so the forecaster distribution has split wide open around an October hold that was already 4-3. Unemployment at 5.7% is the highest since 2016, private wages are 2.0% against 3.7% inflation, and Saturday's election is a genuine binary - Labour has pledged to restore the Reserve Bank's dual mandate, which the market would read as easing over time. Fifth, the metals, which did not move together. Gold is 4047.86 and minus 0.97% on the day but plus 4.44% on the week, a roughly 250-dollar week off the October 30 low near 3,869.85 that touched about 4,146.63 during Thursday's rout; today's pullback is positioning into the last payrolls before December, not a change of regime, and the regime - a two-month-low real yield and a Fed whose December odds just fell a sixth - is intact. Silver is 51.361 and minus 0.81%, plus 5.03% on the week and still minus 14.04% on the month, and it is the one metal with both legs pointing opposite ways: the haven leg matched gold this week while the industrial leg is the one the tech rout damaged. Copper has only the damaged leg. Sixth, the two equity indices, which have genuinely parted company and must not be scored together. The DAX is 26,125.40 and minus 0.43%, which is a remarkably contained response to a 6.36% Nasdaq session, and it is plus 4.07% on the month. The Euro Stoxx 50 is 6,163.70 and minus 0.29% on the day but minus 0.27% on the month against the DAX's plus 4.07%. Banks are the heaviest sector in the EU50 and a live ECB December hike on a 4.0% print is the one leg working for it; that leg is not winning, because the index has gone nowhere in a month while the German index has added four percent, and what is dominating is the rest of the book plus the French and Italian political risk the DAX does not carry. Both are ranges today rather than the longs they were yesterday, because every tailwind in yesterday's case - falling Brent, falling German gas, a dovish-drifting ECB - turned around. The trades that follow from all of this are the ones where a four-notch score gap sits on a leg that broke for a named reason and has no scheduled repair: AUD/CHF, NZD/CHF, and on three notches EUR/AUD, GBP/AUD and AUD/JPY. The things to leave alone are crude in either direction and anything that needs payrolls to land a particular way.

today.headline: Employment fell 4,700 against a plus 14,600 forecast and unemployment rose to a six-month-high 6.7% - the second job-loss month running.
today.read: Cut from zero to minus one. The print was soft in level and worse in composition: the unemployment rate rose to 6.7% from 6.5% against a 6.5% forecast with the participation rate unchanged at 64.8%, so this is genuine slack and not a bigger labour force; full-time employment fell 18,100 while part-time rose 13,400, wholesale and retail trade shed 28,800 against a construction gain of 16,000, and youth unemployment rose 0.7 points to 13.7%. That removes the domestic case for a December 9 hike - one JPMorgan-linked note had it near 50/50 beforehand - and leaves TradingEconomics' 2.50% December forecast looking close to settled. The price was kinder than the data because the dollar was busy elsewhere in the same minute: US payrolls printed 165,000 against a 65,000 forecast with unemployment down to 4.1%, DXY is 102.185 and plus 0.63%, so USD/CAD at 1.40951 and plus 0.54% says more about the dollar than the loonie, while EUR/CAD and GBP/CAD sit within 0.1% of flat and the loonie is still firmer against the two weakest currencies at AUD/CAD minus 0.49% and NZD/CAD minus 0.59%. The forward lean follows from that: the cleaner way to own a softer loonie is now against the currencies that still have live tightening - the euro, sterling and the yen - rather than against the Aussie and the Kiwi, where the score gap has narrowed to a single notch. The next risk is crude, because WTI at 91.114 and plus 0.66% is the only thing still holding the Bank's inflation story together, and the December 4 labour force survey is the test of whether two negative months become three.

today.read: Downgraded from minus one to minus two, and the evidence is the crosses plus a named transmission rather than a forecast. AUD/USD is 0.68810 and minus 0.70%, minus 2.15% on the week; AUD/CHF is minus 0.76% and minus 3.19% on the week, the largest weekly move of any cross on this board; AUD/JPY minus 0.68%, AUD/CAD minus 0.53%, AUD/NZD minus 0.06%, with EUR/AUD plus 0.53% and GBP/AUD plus 0.54%. The reason is no longer an inference. Copper is 6.1867, minus 1.00% on the day, minus 4.21% on the week and minus 6.21% on the month, and ANZ attributes the weakness to the technology selloff weighing on sentiment - which is precisely the AI-related demand for technology goods that the RBA listed in its own November 3 statement as a reason to hike. The Nasdaq 100's 6.36% session is the same shock arriving through a different instrument. Against that the RBA holds the highest cash rate on this board at 4.85%, delivered on a 6-3 vote with three members preferring a hold, and softened its commitment to further tightening while Bullock declined any forward guidance. A top policy rate that the market will not pay for, sitting on a demand leg being dismantled in public, is the cleanest short here. The one leg that turned in Australia's favour today is fuel, and it is not the leg that is hurting. Watch the November 17 minutes for whether the three holdouts have become four.

today.headline: Beat all seven other currencies on the day and all seven on the week, and the energy rebound repaired the inflation leg this file cut yesterday.
today.read: Upgraded from plus one to plus two. The price is unambiguous on both horizons: USD/CHF 0.81615 and minus 0.06% on the day and minus 1.07% on the week, EUR/CHF 0.91388 and minus 0.25% and minus 0.78%, GBP/CHF 1.09566 and minus 0.24% and minus 0.82%, AUD/CHF minus 0.76% and minus 3.19%, NZD/CHF minus 0.66% and minus 2.30%, CAD/CHF minus 0.25% and minus 1.59%, CHF/JPY 193.299 and plus 0.09% and plus 1.20%. The franc is near its highest since mid-September. For the first time in a fortnight it has both legs at once: equities are in correction after the Nasdaq 100's 6.36% rout, and the Strait is being attacked again with the IRGC reporting two tankers and a tugboat burned. The inflation leg is the part that changed from yesterday. The October 1.5% CPI that earned an upgrade on Wednesday and a downgrade on Thursday was roughly 96% energy, and the downgrade rested on that energy falling - EU gas is now plus 1.99% on the day and plus 18.44% on the month, so the Q1/27 pass-through case is better than it looked twenty-four hours ago. What keeps this at plus two rather than plus three is the central bank, not the data: the SNB is at zero, Schlegel said Thursday the policy rate remains the main tool and he has not yet seen significant second-round effects, no near-term hike is expected, and Commerzbank reads current EUR/CHF levels as approaching where the SNB has previously threatened stronger intervention. The franc has the momentum and the SNB owns the ceiling.

today.headline: Citi scrapped its RBNZ hike forecasts outright while the Kiwi slid to 0.55604, and the country votes on Saturday.
today.read: Held at minus two, with the composition of the case changing rather than its level. NZD/USD is 0.55604 and minus 0.60%, minus 1.24% on the week; NZD/CHF minus 0.66% and minus 2.30%, NZD/JPY minus 0.55%, NZD/CAD minus 0.42%, and AUD/NZD minus 0.06% means the Kiwi actually outperformed the Aussie on the day and by 0.91% on the week. The new information is the forecaster distribution rather than the price. Citi has dropped its RBNZ tightening calls entirely and now expects the OCR on hold through 2027, a view weaker than the Bank's own guidance; Commerzbank still looks for hikes in December and the first quarter of 2027; ANZ looks for 25 basis points at each of the next three meetings. A spread that wide on a meeting five weeks away, around an October hold that was already 4-3, is the signal. The hard data supports the dovish end: unemployment 5.7%, the highest since 2016, private wages 2.0% against 3.7% inflation, employment minus 0.1% on the quarter. The hawkish end rests on the RBNZ's 4.4% December inflation forecast, which is a fuel pass-through forecast - and fuel turned back up today, which firms that leg for the first time this week. Saturday's vote sits on top as a true binary: a close National-Labour race where Labour has pledged to restore the Bank's dual mandate, which would be read as easing over time. Short the Kiwi against the franc and the euro rather than against the Aussie, and size for the weekend.

today.headline: December hike odds fell from about 82% to 67% on an equity rout rather than on any data, and the dollar rose anyway.
today.read: Held at zero, and the reason it is held is worth stating because both legs inverted. Yesterday this entry read weak price, firming rate case. Today it is firm price, fading rate case. DXY is 101.757 and plus 0.15%, minus 0.12% on the week, and the dollar beat five of seven - EUR/USD 1.11977 and minus 0.19%, GBP/USD 1.34250 and minus 0.18%, USD/CAD 1.40455 and plus 0.19%, AUD/USD minus 0.70%, NZD/USD minus 0.60% - losing only to the yen, with USD/JPY at 157.776 and plus 0.05%, and to the franc. CME FedWatch reads 66% to 68% against 82% a day earlier, Kalshi and Polymarket are near 66% with a hold near 31%, and the ten-year fell to about 4.837%, a two-month low against an October high of 5.36%. This file carried 76% to 82% yesterday and that has to be withdrawn. The cause was not data and not the Fed: the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36% and erased roughly 2.3 trillion dollars as the midterm sweep was re-read as regulatory drag on data-centre buildout, Democrats having also taken the Texas and Ohio governorships, and the flight into Treasuries repriced December. The domestic case is intact and still the only hawkish case on this board that never needed energy - CPI 3.7%, core 2.6%, two October dissents for a hike. today.headline: Bought as a haven against the breaking of its own hike premise, gaining on five of seven while losing to the dollar and the franc.
today.read: Held at plus one and MIXED, and the tension is the point rather than a hedge. The yen gained against the euro, sterling, the Aussie, the Kiwi and the Canadian dollar - EUR/JPY 176.658 and minus 0.15%, GBP/JPY 211.794 and minus 0.14%, AUD/JPY 108.5480 and minus 0.68%, NZD/JPY 87.7300 and minus 0.55%, CAD/JPY 112.3280 and minus 0.14% - and lost marginally to the dollar at 157.776 and to the franc, with CHF/JPY plus 0.09% and plus 1.20% on the week. So it won the risk-off against the risk currencies and lost it to the two other havens. The policy case reads strong on the surface: hawkish minutes this week, swaps near 80% for December 18, more than 80% of economists expecting 1.50%, and TradingEconomics forecasting 1.50%. The problem underneath is that Ueda's stated reason for tightening leaned on strong global AI demand, and that is exactly what lost roughly 2.3 trillion dollars of equity value on Thursday and what ANZ now blames for copper. The Bank is being asked to hike into the breaking of its own premise while its currency is bid for the same reason - which is why this is MIXED at plus one and not an upgrade. Ueda speaks at 16:00Z today, before payrolls lands in full, and he has been vague at the last two outings; a hawkish tone with the AI narrative stripped out of it would be the thing that earns an upgrade. Japan has spent more than 27 trillion yen defending the yen in 2026, a record, and 160 remains the line.

today.headline: Downgraded a second notch as the hike proved spent, but the energy rebound is re-arming the exact condition Bailey set for the next one.
today.read: Cut from plus two to plus one, which is the second cut in two days and in the same direction for the same reason - the path rather than the level. GBP/USD is 1.34250 and minus 0.18%, plus 0.25% on the week; sterling lost to the dollar, the yen and the franc, was flat against the euro at EUR/GBP 0.83407 and minus 0.01% and against the loonie at GBP/CAD plus 0.02%, and gained only on GBP/AUD plus 0.54% and GBP/NZD plus 0.51%. Beating only the two weakest currencies on the board is not a plus-two price. The level is still the strongest case here - Bank Rate at 4.00% on a unanimous hike vote, 8-1 with Mann wanting 0.5 points, and a Monetary Policy Report projecting CPI near 5% by mid-2027 - but the hike is now in the price and Bailey spent his press conference telling the market the curve above 4.00% is risk premia rather than expected rates. What is genuinely new today runs the other way, and it is the reason this is a one-notch cut rather than two. Bailey made the next increase conditional on there being no progress towards resolving the Middle East conflict. There has been no progress - the IRGC burned two tankers and a tugboat in the Strait - and UK gas is 230.35, plus 2.41% on the day and plus 18.97% on the month, with Brent back near 100. He wrote the trigger for his own next hike and that trigger is arming again rather than disarming. Sterling is a buy against the Aussie and the Kiwi and a hold against everything else until the February pricing moves.

today.headline: The quietest currency on the board: flat against sterling and the loonie, with the December hike case helped by the very energy rebound that hurt everyone else.
today.read: Held at plus one. The euro did almost nothing on its own account - EUR/USD 1.11977 and minus 0.19%, EUR/GBP 0.83407 and minus 0.01%, EUR/CAD 1.57275 and plus 0.01%, EUR/JPY 176.658 and minus 0.15%, EUR/CHF 0.91388 and minus 0.25% - and its only real moves were the mirror image of Australian and New Zealand weakness, with EUR/AUD plus 0.53% and plus 2.55% on the week and EUR/NZD plus 0.57% and plus 1.62%. That is a currency being carried rather than bid, which is why it stays at plus one and MIXED despite holding second place on this board. The forward case firmed slightly today for a reason specific to the euro area. The 4.0% October HICP, a three-year high, was delivered by energy at 20.8%, and the euro-area energy input is gas - which is 92.48 and plus 1.99% on the day and plus 18.44% on the month even after minus 11.03% on the week. Lagarde said in Milan on Thursday that the Council is watching the indirect effects of the energy shock tied to the Iran war and will let the indicators and the new staff projections decide December, while cautioning that the rate tool should not be swung like a hammer; Nagel calls a December hike very likely necessary and Panetta says it may be needed. Pricing cannot be pinned down - sources run from about 72% to roughly 90% - so trade the direction and distrust the level. Core stuck at 2.5% and wage growth down to 3.0% are why this is not an upgrade. Eurostat finalises November 18 and Lagarde departs February 7, 2027.

catalysts.event: United States: Non-Farm Employment Change, Unemployment Rate and Average Hourly Earnings (red folder)
catalysts.note: The last payrolls before the December 9 FOMC, and the resolution of the dollar's inverted legs. Payrolls forecast at plus 65,000 after plus 29,000, unemployment held at 4.2%, average hourly earnings plus 0.3% after plus 0.1%; one wire carries a plus 56,000 consensus instead, so the surprise threshold itself is uncertain. December hike odds have fallen to 66-68% from 82% a day earlier on the equity rout rather than on data, so this print decides whether the dollar's firm price or its fading rate case wins. A beat above about 100,000 rebuilds December and breaks DXY through 102; a miss under 30,000 with equities still falling takes gold higher and the dollar back to its lows.

catalysts.event: Canada: Employment Change and Unemployment Rate (red folder)
catalysts.note: Lands in the same minute as US payrolls, which makes USD/CAD an event trade rather than a thesis trade. Employment forecast at plus 14,600 after minus 68,300, unemployment held at 6.5%; one wire carries plus 13,600. This is the swing input for a December 9 decision that TradingEconomics forecasts as a hold at 2.50%. A beat with WTI holding above 90 puts a December hike back in play after crude stopped deflating; a second consecutive negative print would make the October hike look like the last one. Cleaner expressions of a firmer loonie today are AUD/CAD and NZD/CAD.

catalysts.event: Japan: BoJ Governor Ueda Speaks (red folder)
catalysts.note: The most asymmetric event on this board after payrolls, because the Bank has a contradiction to resolve. December 18 is near 80% priced in swaps with more than 80% of surveyed economists expecting 1.50% and TradingEconomics forecasting it, but Ueda's stated reasoning for tightening leaned on strong global AI demand - which lost roughly 2.3 trillion dollars of equity value on Thursday and which ANZ now blames for copper being down 4.21% on the week. A hawkish tone that no longer rests on the global AI argument would take the yen to plus two and break CHF/JPY, EUR/JPY and GBP/JPY lower. He was vague at his last two outings.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: Parliamentary Elections (red folder)
catalysts.note: Polls open Saturday morning New Zealand time, which is Friday evening UTC. A genuine binary and a weekend gap risk on every Kiwi cross. Polls show a close National-Labour race; Labour has pledged to restore the Reserve Bank's dual mandate, which the market would read as easing over time, and Citi flags a left-leaning result as a risk to investor confidence. It lands into a December 9 meeting on which professional forecasters have split from on-hold-through-2027 at Citi to three consecutive hikes at ANZ. Size NZD/CHF and EUR/NZD for the gap rather than for the score spread.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: Official Bank Rate, MPC Votes, Monetary Policy Summary and Report (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. Bank Rate raised 25 basis points to 4.00% from 3.75%, in line with forecast and the first increase since August 2023, on an 8-1 vote with Catherine Mann preferring 0.5 points to 4.25% - so all nine members wanted a hike, against a 7-0-2 forecast. The Monetary Policy Report has CPI rising to around 5% by the middle of next year, and the Summary repeated that policy is not on a pre-set path. TradingEconomics now carries 4.00% for November. Alan Taylor's framing in the minutes is that this is not the start of a hiking cycle.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: BoE Governor Bailey Press Conference (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released, and it is still driving sterling today. Bailey called the fall in oil prices positive news, said the market curve pricing further restrictiveness into next year largely reflects risk premia rather than expected rates - direct pushback on the 4.25% February median in the Bank's own Market Participants Survey - and made the next increase conditional in one sentence: unless there is progress towards resolving the conflict, a further increase in Bank Rate may be warranted. He declined to cap it from the other side too. What changed overnight is the condition rather than the words: UK gas is plus 2.41% today and plus 18.97% on the month and Brent is back near 100, so the trigger he wrote is arming again.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA Cash Rate, Rate Statement and Monetary Policy Statement (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. Hiked 25 basis points to 4.85% from 4.60%, in line with forecast, on a 6-3 majority - the fifth increase this year and the highest cash rate since late 2008, with three members preferring a hold. The statement cited elevated fuel and commodity prices, tighter domestic capacity and AI-related demand for technology goods, and analysts read it as softening the commitment to further tightening. Two of those three pillars are now being dismantled: copper is minus 4.21% on the week with ANZ attributing it to the technology selloff, and only the fuel pillar turned back in the RBA's favour. TradingEconomics carries 4.85% for November.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA Press Conference with Governor Bullock (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. Bullock declined to provide forward guidance and did not replace the tightening bias the statement dropped, which reads as a pause into February. The market verdict has been unambiguous since: a 4.85% cash rate, the highest on this board, has bought a three-week low below 0.70 and losses against all seven other currencies on two consecutive days.

catalysts.event: United States: Congressional Elections (red folder)
catalysts.note: Resolved as a Democratic sweep of both chambers, and the market has now traded it twice in opposite directions. First as relief on deficit expansion: the Dow jumped about 3% on Wednesday and the ten-year fell. Then, on Thursday, as regulatory drag on AI infrastructure - Democrats also took the Texas and Ohio governorships, among the most intense data-centre development areas - and the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36%, 1,807 points, to 26,629.81, erasing roughly 2.3 trillion dollars, with the Dow down more than 1,800 points and the Russell 2000 down 4.45%. That second reading pulled the ten-year to about 4.837% and December Fed hike odds from 82% to 66-68%.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: Employment Change and Unemployment Rate (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released and still the dominant Kiwi input. Unemployment rose to 5.7%, the highest since 2016 and above the 5.5% forecast, employment fell 0.1% on the quarter against a plus 0.4% forecast, and private wages slowed to 2.0% against 3.7% inflation. Citi has since scrapped its RBNZ hike forecasts entirely and now expects the OCR on hold through 2027, while Commerzbank still looks for December and Q1/27 and ANZ for three consecutive hikes.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ Financial Stability Report
catalysts.note: The first official RBNZ communication after Saturday's election and before the December 9 Monetary Policy Statement. Relevant less for financial stability than for any signal on how the Committee reads a labour market at a ten-year unemployment high against a 4.4% December inflation forecast that rests on fuel pass-through.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA November Meeting Minutes
catalysts.note: The next real test of the Australian short. The November 3 hike carried three of nine preferring a hold; watch whether the holdouts became four and whether the AI-related demand argument survives the week in which the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36% and copper fell 4.21%. Hawkish minutes restoring the dropped tightening bias are the main invalidation for AUD/CHF, EUR/AUD and GBP/AUD.

catalysts.event: Euro area: Final October HICP (Eurostat)
catalysts.note: Confirms or revises the 4.0% flash, a three-year high, and gives the full energy and core breakdown ahead of December 17. The flash had energy at 20.8% against core stuck at 2.5% and monthly momentum easing to plus 0.4%, so the composition matters more than the headline for whether the ECB can justify a hike on something other than gas.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA Cash Rate Decision
catalysts.note: Reads as a pause after five hikes this year to 4.85%, with February the meeting actually being traded. Reports today of collapsed December pricing and of a cut being priced by year-end could not be reconciled across sources and are not relied on here.

catalysts.event: United States: FOMC Decision and new Economic Projections
catalysts.note: A hike remains the modal outcome but at roughly two thirds rather than four fifths after the equity rout took odds from 82% to 66-68%. Today's payrolls is the main input left, and the new projections will show whether the Committee reads the AI capital-spending unwind as disinflationary enough to matter.

catalysts.event: Canada: BoC Decision, and New Zealand: RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement
catalysts.note: TradingEconomics forecasts a BoC hold at 2.50% and an RBNZ hike to 3.00% on the same day. The Canadian call turns on today's jobs print and on whether crude holds above 90; the New Zealand call is the widest forecaster split on this board, from Citi's hold-through-2027 to ANZ's three consecutive hikes, and comes after Saturday's election.

catalysts.event: Switzerland: SNB Policy Rate Decision
catalysts.note: A hold at zero is expected with no TradingEconomics forecast attached. Schlegel said on Thursday that the policy rate remains the main tool, that the bank would step in if price stability were threatened, and that he has not yet seen significant second-round inflation effects. The live question is the second instrument rather than the rate, with the franc near a two-month high. The Quarterly Bulletin follows December 16.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB Decision, and United Kingdom: BoE Decision
catalysts.note: Both final 2026 meetings on the same day. The ECB carries a live hike that today's gas rebound supports, with pricing reported anywhere from 72% to 90% and therefore not verifiable. The BoE is live again only if the energy rebound holds, since Bailey made the next increase conditional on there being no progress towards resolving the Middle East conflict - February remains the modal move on the Bank's own survey median.

catalysts.event: Japan: BoJ Policy Decision
catalysts.note: Near 80% priced in swaps with more than 80% of surveyed economists expecting 1.50% and TradingEconomics forecasting it, after an 8-1 October hold with Takata dissenting for an immediate move. The unresolved question is the one Ueda can address at 16:00Z today: whether the hike case survives without the strong global AI demand argument it has rested on.

catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz: closure, tanker attacks and the Qatar-mediated channel
catalysts.note: The single largest cross-asset risk on this board and now genuinely two-sided within the same session. The IRGC says two tankers and a tugboat were burned in the Strait, which took Brent back to 99.862 and plus 1.60% and the gas complex up 2% to 3%. Simultaneously Iran said it could reopen Hormuz within two days if its demands on sanctions and frozen assets were met, with Qatar mediating and Iran's foreign minister meeting Saudi and Qatari officials. Resolution either way moves crude 5% and reprices the Bank of England, the ECB, the SNB and the Bank of Canada together.

catalysts.event: The AI capital-spending repricing, now an equity event
catalysts.note: It stopped being a commodity and sentiment story on Thursday and became a market event: the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36% and erased roughly 2.3 trillion dollars, the index is in correction, and it was the worst session since the April 2025 tariff panic. The transmission into FX is no longer inferred - ANZ attributes copper's 4.21% weekly fall to the technology selloff, which is the exact AI-related demand the RBA, the BoJ and the RBNZ all cited when they turned hawkish. Watch whether it broadens from chips and data-centre suppliers into European industrials, which is what would turn GER40 from a range into a short.

geopolitics: The Strait of Hormuz is still closed, the premium came out of crude on Wednesday, and today a good part of it went back in - and the reason it went back in is the reason this is not a de-escalation story. Brent is 99.862 and plus 1.60% on the day, back from 94.106 twenty-four hours ago, a 6.1% round trip; WTI is 91.648 and plus 1.25%, up from 87.186, about 4.5% off Wednesday's low. Both remain down roughly 12% on the week, so the great break stands and roughly a third of it has been retraced in two sessions. The gas complex moved further: EU gas 92.48 and plus 1.99% against 85.18 yesterday, German gas 92.13 and plus 2.84%, UK gas 230.35 and plus 2.41%, and while all three are still 7% to 11% lower on the week they are now 18% to 20% higher on the month. The driver is not sentiment. The IRGC says two tankers and a tugboat were burned in the Strait, after Tehran had already sharply increased attacks on shipping and rejected Washington's response to its conditions for reopening on November 4. What makes the risk genuinely two-sided rather than simply hawkish is that the diplomatic channel moved in the same session: Iran said it could reopen Hormuz within two days if its demands on sanctions and frozen assets were met, Qatar is mediating, and Iran's foreign minister met Saudi and Qatari officials. So the market is being asked to price a reopening within days and an escalating tanker war at the same time, which is exactly why USOIL is a level trade at 91 rather than a direction in either sense, and why resolution either way is worth about 5% on crude. The FX transmission has now flipped back to the configuration it held all autumn, and it runs through six of these eight currencies. Bailey made the next Bank of England increase conditional in one sentence - unless there is progress towards resolving the conflict, a further increase in Bank Rate may be warranted - and with UK gas plus 18.97% on the month and two tankers burning, there is no progress; he wrote his own trigger and it is arming. The euro area's 4.0% October HICP was delivered by energy at 20.8% against core stuck at 2.5%, Lagarde said on Thursday that the Council is watching the indirect effects of the energy shock tied to the Iran war, and euro-area gas up 18.44% on the month is that shock continuing into the November and December prints. The franc's October 1.5% CPI was roughly 96% energy, so the pass-through case this file cut yesterday is partly repaired today. Macklem's Middle East energy shock has stopped deflating, which stabilises the Canadian case without re-arming it while TradingEconomics still forecasts a December hold. The RBNZ's 4.4% December inflation forecast rests on fuel pass-through and firmed for the first time this week. Only the RBA gets no help, because its problem is the other commodity: copper is minus 4.21% on the week and ANZ ties that directly to the technology selloff. And the franc keeps the haven bid on both legs at once - the Strait being attacked again, and an equity market in correction after the Nasdaq 100's 6.36% session - which is why it beat all seven other majors on the day and on the week, with the SNB rather than the data as its ceiling.
